Are big companies controlling what we eat? | AUT Food Politics Matters

Welcome to Auckland University of Technology’s (AUT) Research Matters! 🚀 AUT’s Research Matters video series is where AUT academics answer everyday questions about their fields of expertise. Get the answer to those questions you’ve always had – or maybe never knew to ask. 

Do you ever get the uneasy feeling that big business is controlling your food? 🍫🌍 From seeds and supply chains to supermarket shelves and “health” claims, food politics shapes what ends up on our plates - but it’s not always easy to spot.  

Why is “healthy” food so expensive? And why is it so hard to tell what’s actually good for you from the label? Tracy Berno, a professor at AUT, is unpacking what food politics is, what’s wrong with the global food system, and what we can realistically do as individuals in the latest episode of Food Politics Matters.

Webinar: Get more from your EROAD telematics

Fuel efficiency is one of the biggest opportunities for fleet operators right now - and with the right data, small improvements can translate into meaningful savings over time. That’s where telematics comes in.

EECA has partnered with National Road Carriers Association (Inc) and EROAD to deliver a practical webinar for fleet managers looking to get more from their telematics. Whether you’re already using the technology or just starting to explore it, this session shows you how to better monitor, manage, and optimise fuel use without compromising productivity.

In this session, Matt Buckle, NZ Enterprise Sales Manager with EROAD covers:

• Fuel use and idling - identify opportunities to reduce waste and switch off
• Off-road reporting and RUC refunds - claim refunds quickly and accurately
• Fuel efficiency benchmarking - compare performance across similar vehicles
• Driver log-on and leaderboards - encourage and reward efficient driving behaviour
• Fuel exceptions - get alerts for unusual consumption or purchases

Wellington air ambulance simulator

Ever wondered how our teams train for real emergencies in the air?

Wellington Regional Hospital is home to a little-known gem: a flight simulator modelled on a real air ambulance aircraft. The simulator and its equipment allow health professionals, including doctors, nurses and midwives, to sharpen their skills and strengthen patient safety during transfers. It is used by teams from across New Zealand to practise responding to high-stakes situations where lives are on the line.

This training was made possible thanks to the incredible support of the Wellington Hospitals Foundation, their generous donors, and their Founding Chair at the time, Bill Day. We are deeply grateful for their commitment to helping our teams deliver the best care possible. Their support has an impact not only in the Wellington region but nationwide, as health professionals from all over New Zealand benefit from this simulator.

Waltham Maintenance Hub opening

on March 24, we were proud to join key stakeholders to welcome the Minister for Rail, Rt Hon Winston Peters, who officially opened the new state of the art Waltham Maintenance Hub in Christchurch, delivered through a $110 million Government investment.
 
The event also showcased the first of the new low emission, higher powered DM locomotives, currently being built by Stadler in Spain. The Government has committed $533 million for 66 DM locomotives, with 47 replacing the ageing South Island fleet, as part of a wider $1.2 billion investment in South Island rail since 2019.
 
The Waltham hub provides a modern, safe and efficient working environment for our people and will support maintenance of KiwiRail’s locomotives, wagons and passenger carriages operating across the South Island.
 
More efficient maintenance, combined with a more reliable and modern locomotive fleet, will deliver better, more consistent services for our South Island customers and we’re excited about what this means for the continued growth of rail in the South.

AI Haumaru, AI Motuhake mō te Māori GIS kaupapa

Safe, secure, sovereign AI for Māori GIS projects

AI is showing up everywhere. Some of it is useful, some of it is risky, and much of it isn’t explained in ways that make sense for iwi and hapū GIS contexts.

In this video, GIS Specialist Duane Wilkins shares practical tools and techniques that can be applied across a range of Māori GIS mapping kaupapa. Whether you're new to AI or already experimenting, this kōrero focuses on real-world use rather than theory, helping you apply AI in ways that make sense for your mahi.

Learn how to use AI in ways that protect your data, strengthen your mapping capability, and uphold the integrity of your work on the whenua.

You’ll gain a clear, jargon-free understanding of what AI tools actually do, along with practical ways to safely trial AI on your own computer without exposing sensitive information. The session also explores how AI can speed up mapping, reporting, and data preparation while highlighting key risks around privacy, ownership, and external platforms.

This video is especially relevant for iwi and hapū working with whenua and data, Māori trusts and organisations managing land and assets, GIS practitioners wanting practical and accessible approaches to AI, and anyone responsible for data who wants to better understand the risks before using these tools.

Using AI without understanding it can put your data at risk, while ignoring it entirely means missing out on tools that can save time and support better decision-making.

You’ll leave with a clearer understanding of how AI can support your kaupapa — and where to draw the line to protect your data, your people, and your work.

Te Mārama ki ngā Rū Whenua - Using Earthquake and Earth Science Data for Māori GIS & Mapping Kaupapa

Every rohe carries its own history of rū whenua, from small shifts to major events that shape our whenua and communities. This wānanga will help you access and use real earth science data to better understand those patterns, support safer planning, and strengthen kaitiakitanga. This is a practical session with Jonathan Hanson, the GeoNet Data manager, from Earth Sciences New Zealand, focused on turning national datasets into useful tools for iwi, hapū, and Māori organisations. Jonathan shows how you can easily overlay this data with your own and other datasets to support whenua management, risk awareness, and planning.

What you will learn
- What GeoNet/Earth Science NZ datasets are available and how they relate to Māori interests
- How to find and use earthquake, tsunami, and volcano data for whenua and taiao decision making
- How to bring earth science data into your own Māori GIS mapping kaupapa

Example datasets covered
- Earthquake data for hazard awareness and historical analysis
- Tsunami Gauge Network for coastal monitoring and response planning
- Volcano cameras for real time environmental observation
- Sensor Map tools for exploring monitoring infrastructure

Why this matters for Māori
- Strengthen decision making for whenua and taiao using trusted data
- Support kaitiakitanga with both real time and historical environmental insights
- Build internal capability to use national datasets within iwi and hapū contexts
- Improve planning and preparedness for natural hazards across rohe and communities

Accessing Council GIS Maps, Data and Resources: Bay of Plenty Regional Council BayMaps a Case Study

This Ngā Poutama Matawhenua webinar explores how local government geospatial and GIS data can support mahi, with a focus on the Bay of Plenty Regional Council BayMaps resources.

Georgia Edwards, GIS Analyst at Bay of Plenty Regional Council, demonstrates a range of BayMaps resources including Resource Consents, Marae Locations, BayHazards, the Sea Level Rise Tool, the Historic Imagery Swipe Tool, Bay eXplorer, and the data download page. The session shows how these tools and datasets can be used to access council maps, download data, use data services to keep information current, and bring layers together for practical mapping and analysis.

The session is aimed at iwi, hapū, Māori organisations, trusts, and whānau who want to better understand the kinds of geospatial and GIS data that local and regional councils collect and make available online.

Recorded on Friday 27 March 2026 as part of the 2026 Ngā Poutama Matawhenua webinar series.

Waltham Maintenance Hub opening

on March 24, we were proud to join key stakeholders to welcome the Minister for Rail, Rt Hon Winston Peters, who officially opened the new state of the art Waltham Maintenance Hub in Christchurch, delivered through a $110 million Government investment.
 
The event also showcased the first of the new low emission, higher powered DM locomotives, currently being built by Stadler in Spain. The Government has committed $533 million for 66 DM locomotives, with 47 replacing the ageing South Island fleet, as part of a wider $1.2 billion investment in South Island rail since 2019.
 
The Waltham hub provides a modern, safe and efficient working environment for our people and will support maintenance of KiwiRail’s locomotives, wagons and passenger carriages operating across the South Island.
 
More efficient maintenance, combined with a more reliable and modern locomotive fleet, will deliver better, more consistent services for our South Island customers and we’re excited about what this means for the continued growth of rail in the South.

KiwiRail Alicetown Mural

Feilding artist Joe Mcmenamin has been doing some great work around the Wellington Metro, helping to make your trip just a little bit more beautiful.

He’s been turning bland walls and signal boxes into stunning canvases to “bring nature into the city.”

“I love painting New Zealand birds and forest and enjoy painting them on murals for the public to enjoy,” Joe says.

Joe recently painted a collection of larger-than-life native birds on a signal hut in Alicetown.

Please note that due to the location of this signal box, minimal PPE was required. Please remember that Joe was invited by KiwiRail to do this work. Entering KiwiRail land without the correct permission is both extremely illegal and unsafe.

Head Start: simplifying local government

Here’s a quick update from Mayor Andrew on the Head Start work currently underway 👆

The Government’s Head Start programme gives councils across New Zealand a three-month window to come up with proposals for reorganising local government in their regions - this is the Head Start pathway.

We are already having early conversations with key partners to better understand what this could mean for Whanganui and will reach out to the wider community as this work develops.

Mayor Andrew says it’s important to take the time to get the foundations right, rather than rush to a solution.

“This is not just a technical discussion about boundaries or structures. For Whanganui, it is also about identity, relationships, representation, service delivery, and how we protect and advance the wellbeing of Whanganui for future generations.”

“We’re committed to keeping the community updated as we work through this and we’re keen to hear what people have to say.”

Updates, information and future consultation opportunities will be shared on this Facebook page and on the Head Start page on our website - whanganui.govt.nz

Morningside Flood Relief Scheme

We are so pleased to see the difference this project is making for the Morningside community!

In the past, the area frequently experienced flooding when heavy rainfall coincided with high tides. This project has transformed the catchment into a more controlled and resilient stormwater system, using a combination of gravity diversion and managed pumping.

Delivered by WDC, Weir Consultants, and United Civil, the project is helping reduce flooding, improve environmental outcomes, and shows how smart, collaborative stormwater solutions can be delivered within tight timeframes and budgets.
